transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-11-10 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Leo (Redwood SE), Evan (Grailpoint CTO), Priya (Grailpoint ML Eng), Sam (Infra)

Summary:
Quick discovery / sprint kickoff to evaluate Redwood's self-serve API (PLG path) vs Dedicated/Private pilot. Customer wants to understand time-to-first-token (TTFT), what we include in the free credits quickstart, and security boundary for VPC/private deployment. Agreed next step: Redwood to provide credits + quickstart guide, run a benchmark with Leo and Grailpoint sample prompts, and clarify audit/KMS questions.

Topics:
- Quickstart credits and expected TTFT
- Hosted API tradeoffs (latency vs cost)
- Dedicated pools / reserved capacity for production
- Private (VPC/on-prem) security controls (KMS, audit logs, SSO)
- Pilot success metrics and timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we really appreciate the time. quick intro, I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the account, with me is Leo our SE who will run the benchmark. how are you all?
[00:12] Evan: good, thanks. this is Evan, CTO at Grailpoint. we want to make sure we can get a live prototype within two weeks and then a small pilot in a month.
[00:20] Priya: hi, priya here. i'm the ml engineer, focused on model outputs and quality, we also care about the inference cost per 1k tokens.
[00:28] Sam: sam, infra — i'm mostly concerned about VPC connectivity and whether we can keep logs inside our account.
[00:34] Leo: great, thanks all. quick agenda: credits and quickstart path, demo of the API surface at a high level, security Qs, and then a short scoping on the benchmark we'll run. sound good?
[00:44] Evan: yep.

[01:05] Maya: first, our PLG path: we offer free credits for 30 to 60 days depending on scope, that includes enough tokens to run a TTFT sprint. typical TTFT for a simple text gen test is under an hour from signup if you follow the quickstart. but there are caveats — network setup, auth and sample prompts matter.
[01:25] Evan: okay under an hour is ideal. what exactly is in the quickstart? like do you provide sample scripts, SDKs, a docker run?
[01:34] Maya: yes we provide SDK snippets in python/js, curl examples, an infra checklist for VPC peering if you want private connectivity, and a sample benchmark harness. we'll attach a playbook. also we include a small amount of hosted credits by default, and if you need more for a demo we'll bump it to 60 days.
[01:52] Priya: does the hosted credits mean data leaves our VPC? we're cautious about sending PHI.
[01:58] Leo: good callout — our hosted API is multi-tenant but we offer options: encrypted-in-transit, and we have data retention policies configurable per account. if you need zero-data-retention we can enable that on the account so inputs are not stored. for regulated data we often recommend the private deployment or dedicated pools with customer-managed keys.
[02:20] Sam: how does KMS integration work in the private offering? can we bring our own keys?
[02:25] Leo: yes for Redwood Private you can integrate with your KMS/HSM. we support BYOK workflows; keys stay in your cloud account and we only reference them. some on-prem installs have HSM integration too. in the hosted flow we manage keys but we do offer encryption at rest and customer-controlled deletion policies. sometimes the transcript says "kay em ess" as KMS got misheard.

[03:10] Maya: timeline wise: sign up, run quickstart — TTFT within a few hours, benchmark with SE within a week, pilot start once security checklist items are cleared. what's your target timeline?
[03:22] Evan: two weeks to prototype, as I said. pilot within four to six weeks would be great.

[03:40] Priya: okay on technical requirements — we use a mix of short prompts and long context for reranking, sequences up to 2k tokens but most are 200-400 tokens. QPS will start low (1-5 rps) but spike occasionally during ingestion windows. latency SLO we'd like to aim for p95 < 300ms for simple generation, can Redwood hit that on hosted?
[04:02] Leo: that's a common ask. On hosted, with optimized kernels and continuous batching we often hit sub-200ms p95 for smaller models at modest QPS. for consistent sub-300ms at scale you might choose a dedicated pool so you don't contend with other tenants and can pin instance types. there's always a trade-off: dedicated reduces variance but costs more.
[04:28] Sam: and what about cost profiles, like per token or per request math?
[04:33] Maya: hosted is usage-based: token units for generation/embeddings etc. Dedicated is reserved capacity with predictable throughput and a monthly commit. we can share a rough calculator in the playbook.

[05:05] Evan: can you do an A/B where we start hosted for prototyping and then move to dedicated if it is promising? how seamless is that?
[05:12] Leo: very seamless — same API, same model catalog, you can pin model versions and change routing policy. Redwood's smart routing will send traffic to dedicated pool when available and fall back to compatible hosted variants. we can demo the rollout policy later.

[06:00] Priya: about the model catalog — do you host open models or proprietary ones? we want to evaluate model quality and latency tradeoffs.
[06:07] Maya: we have a model catalog with curated open weights and a few partner binaries. you can bring-your-own-model in private deployments. for quickstart we preselect models that are cost-effective and low-latency.

[06:45] Sam: security: SOC2, audit logs, SSO — do you have SAML SSO and per-route audit logs? we'd need traces for compliance reviews.
[06:54] Leo: yes SAML/SSO (we sometimes hear sam-el), RBAC for team roles, and audit logs that can be exported to your SIEM. For private/VPC installs audit logs can be kept entirely on-prem. we'll attach our security pack — it has SOC2 cert details and our encryption docs.

[07:20] Maya: let's scope the benchmark — Leo will run a latency/cost/throughput run with your sample prompts. Priya, can you share ~200-500 prompts that represent the 3 main patterns (short Qs, long context QA, reranking)? Sam share expected QPS and any network constraints.
[07:39] Priya: yes I can share that by Friday, it's about 10k tokens worth of examples.
[07:44] Sam: I can share our VPC diagram, we use AWS and would prefer VPC peering for the private pilot.

[08:10] Leo: perfect. for the benchmark we'll test hosted first with default settings, then a dedicated pool simulation. That will show latencies, token cost, and throughput. We'll also show caching advantages if you have common prefixes.
[08:26] Priya: caching — can you do prefix caching? we have a lot of repeated prompt prefixes for template evaluation.
[08:32] Leo: yes KV cache and prefix caching are part of the runtime optimizations; sometimes the transcript shows it as K V cache or key vee cache. It reduces per-token compute for repeated prefixes.

[09:00] Evan: on the quickstart, are there SDKs and integration samples for our stack? we run python microservices and a node frontend.
[09:07] Maya: yes python and node SDKs, plus a docker example and a small lambda example if you want serverless. We'll include an exportable Postman/Insomnia collection.

[09:36] Sam: about private deployment — what's the minimum lead time and hardware footprint? if we do on-prem we need an ops plan.
[09:45] Leo: private on-prem varies by scale, but a minimal pilot can be done with 2-4 GPUs; for production you'd size by throughput. lead time depends on security review — typically 4-8 weeks for on-prem packaging. VPC/private cloud deployments can be faster — 2-4 weeks if networking approvals are quick.

[10:15] Priya: for pilot success metrics — I propose: p95 latency <300ms for 200-token generations at our baseline QPS, throughput to handle 10rps burst for 60s, and cost per 1k tokens under our target (we'll give target numbers in the doc). if those are hit, we move to pilot.
[10:33] Maya: sounds reasonable. we'll codify that in the pilot scope doc.

[11:00] Evan: procurement — what's the easiest way to start without an enterprise contract? can we do self-serve with credits then move to committed dedicated later?
[11:09] Maya: absolutely. PLG/self-serve with credits is the standard. you can start with hosted credits, run the experiment, and when ready sign a reserved capacity for Dedicated. We'll also provide temporary non-prod dedicated pools for pilots when needed.

[11:40] Priya: any gotchas when moving from hosted to dedicated around model parity? do we have to rewire prompts or retune?
[11:48] Leo: no code changes generally. model versions and quantization differences can alter quality slightly, so we recommend an eval suite run during the cutover. Redwood Optimize will give recommendations on quantization and model variant decisions tied to evaluation prompts.

[12:20] Maya: ok real quick let's go through the checklist of what we need from you to get the TTFT sprint going: sample prompts, expected QPS, contact for networking, sign-off on quickstart credits, and which security docs you need.
[12:35] Priya: we'll share prompts and sample dataset by Friday; QPS is 1-5 typical, 10 for bursts; security docs we need SOC2 and details on KMS/BYOK and data retention.
[12:50] Sam: I will send VPC peering diagram and infra contacts, also who to talk within legal for DPA.

[13:10] Evan: pricing — can you give a ballpark for hosted cost vs dedicated monthly?
[13:15] Maya: ballpark: hosted is pay-as-you-go so for prototyping it's lower upfront but at scale per-token cost can be higher. dedicated usually requires a monthly commit; for rough numbers we'll include a calculator in the follow-up email. I don't want to quote exact numbers in this call without confirming model and QPS.

[14:00] Priya: one more question on observability — how granular are the traces? we want per-request token breakdown and cost attribution to route/model.
[14:08] Leo: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, traces and spans, and you can tag routes to correlate cost. We'll show screenshots in the playbook.

[14:40] Maya: any other open risks?
[14:45] Priya: model hallucination is a concern; we'll need quality guardrails.
[14:48] Leo: we have reranking, evals and quality monitoring. Redwood Optimize ties regressions to prompt sets and can send alerts if quality drifts.

[15:10] Evan: ok good. recap of next steps? Maya you send credits and quickstart; Leo will run benchmark; Priya and Sam share artifacts.
[15:19] Maya: correct. I'll send the email today with attachments and the credits.
[15:25] Leo: I'll ping and book a 1-hour slot for the benchmark, likely week of Nov 16th.
[15:30] Priya: sounds good.
[15:35] Sam: yes thanks.

[16:00] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with a single email summarizing the pilot scope and the action items.
[16:08] Evan: thanks.
[16:12] End of call

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-hear of acronyms (SAML -> sam-el, KMS -> kay em ess), speaker overlaps, and some filler words preserved.
